Section 4.4 of Lock⁵ asks what actually happens when we run a hypothesis
test. Every test can end in one of **two errors**: a **Type I error** rejects
a null hypothesis $H_0$ that is actually true, and a **Type II error** fails
to reject an $H_0$ that is actually false. The **significance level**
$\alpha$ is the price we set in advance for a Type I error — if $H_0$ is
true, results this extreme occur with probability $\alpha$, so about
$\alpha$ of all tests run on true nulls will wrongly find significance
(run 100 tests at $\alpha = 0.05$ on situations where nothing is going on
and about 5 will be "significant" by chance alone). The probability of a
Type II error is $\beta$, and the **power** of a test, $1 - \beta$, is its
ability to detect an effect that is really there. Power grows with the
**sample size** (less chance noise, smaller standard errors) and with the
**effect size** (bigger effects hide less easily), and it also depends on
how much variability there is in the population and on the significance
level chosen. Two further themes run through this section: a small
**p-value is evidence, not proof** — it is the probability, computed
*assuming* $H_0$ is true, of seeing a statistic as extreme as the one
observed, and it is never the probability that $H_0$ is true — and
**statistical significance is not practical significance**: with a big
enough sample even a trivial effect becomes "significant." Running **many
tests** makes all of this worse: at level $\alpha$, about $\alpha$ × (number
of tests) false positives are expected when all nulls are true, so a single
significant hit out of dozens of attempts deserves suspicion, and results
earn trust only through **replication**.
The exercises below are from *Statistics: Unlocking the Power of Data*
(Lock⁵, 3rd ed., pp. 343–348). Skill Builders 4.147–4.150 watch the same
statistic gain strength as sample sizes grow; 4.151–4.154 count expected
false positives; 4.155–4.159 interpret p-values and choose sensible
significance levels; 4.160–4.165 pick large or small $\alpha$ in context;
4.166–4.175 translate Type I and Type II errors into real situations;
and 4.176–4.183 confront the problem of multiple tests and replication,
with a full randomization analysis of the `MateChoice` fruit fly data.
All p-values below come from randomization distributions simulated with
seed 2026 (10,000 replicates unless noted); for tests of a proportion the
null distribution is simulated directly, and for differences in proportions
the shuffle is computed exactly through the hypergeometric count of
successes landing in one group.

```{python}
#| include: false
import os
from pathlib import Path
_root = Path.cwd()
while not (_root / "_quarto.yml").exists():
    _root = _root.parent
os.chdir(_root)
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

REPS = 10000

def rand_prop_p(k, n, seed=2026):
    """P-value (one-tailed, Ha: p > 0.5) for a test of H0: p = 0.5, using the
    randomization distribution of the sample proportion."""
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    sims = r.binomial(n, 0.5, REPS) / n
    return float((sims >= k / n - 1e-12).mean())

def shuffle_diff_stats(k1, n1, k2, n2, seed=2026):
    """Randomization distribution of p-hat1 - p-hat2 under H0: p1 = p2,
    by shuffling the pooled successes (exact hypergeometric shuffle)."""
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    N, K = n1 + n2, k1 + k2
    s1 = r.hypergeometric(K, N - K, n1, REPS)
    return s1 / n1 - (K - s1) / n2

def rand_diff_p(k1, n1, k2, n2, two=False, seed=2026):
    """P-value for a difference in proportions from the shuffle distribution."""
    stat = shuffle_diff_stats(k1, n1, k2, n2, seed)
    obs = k1 / n1 - k2 / n2
    if two:
        return float((np.abs(stat) >= abs(obs) - 1e-12).mean())
    return float((stat >= obs - 1e-12).mean())

def rand_plot(stats_list, obs_list, titles, xlabel, figsize=(7, 2.6)):
    """Row of randomization-distribution histograms with observed statistic lines."""
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(stats_list), figsize=figsize)
    for ax, st, ob, ti in zip(np.atleast_1d(axes), stats_list, obs_list, titles):
        sns.histplot(x=st, bins=30, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
        ax.axvline(ob, color="#c44e52", lw=2)
        ax.set_title(ti, fontsize=10)
        ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Exercise 4.147

*(Skill Builder 1: the same statistic, three sample sizes.)* Testing
$H_0: p = 0.5$ vs $H_a: p > 0.5$ using $\hat p = 0.55$ every time. The
statistic never changes — what changes is the **standard error**. A larger
$n$ makes the randomization distribution (centered at 0.5) narrower, so the
observed 0.55 falls deeper into its tail:

- **(a) $n = 100$: p-value ≈ 0.19 — not significant at a 5% level.**
- **(b) $n = 500$: p-value ≈ 0.013 — significant at a 5% level.**
- **(c) $n = 1000$: p-value ≈ 0.001 — significant, and the strongest
  evidence.**
- **The largest sample size, (c), provides the strongest evidence** for
  $H_a$: same statistic, smaller SE, more extreme, smaller p-value.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Randomization distributions of the sample proportion 0.55 when p = 0.5, for sample sizes 100, 500 and 1000
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7, 2.6))
for ax, n, lab in [(axes[0], 100, "n = 100: p-value = 0.19"),
                   (axes[1], 500, "n = 500: p-value = 0.013"),
                   (axes[2], 1000, "n = 1000: p-value = 0.001")]:
    sims = rng.binomial(n, 0.5, REPS) / n
    sns.histplot(x=sims, bins=30, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
    ax.axvline(0.55, color="#c44e52", lw=2)
    ax.set_title(lab, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("Randomization sample proportions")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.DataFrame({
    "Case": ["(a)", "(b)", "(c)"],
    "Sample size": [100, 500, 1000],
    "Statistic": ["55/100 = 0.55", "275/500 = 0.55", "550/1000 = 0.55"],
    "Randomization p-value": [f"{rand_prop_p(k, n):.3f}"
                              for k, n in [(55, 100), (275, 500), (550, 1000)]],
    "Significant at 5%?": ["No", "Yes", "Yes (strongest)"],
}).to_string()
```

## Exercise 4.149

*(Skill Builder 1: difference in proportions.)* Testing
$H_0: p_1 = p_2$ vs $H_a: p_1 > p_2$ using
$\hat p_1 - \hat p_2 = 0.8 - 0.7 = 0.10$:

- **(a) $n_1 = 30$, $n_2 = 20$: p-value ≈ 0.32 — not significant.** The
  shuffle distribution is wide (and quite discrete at these sizes; a normal
  approximation would put the p-value near 0.21 — either way, nowhere near
  0.05).
- **(b) $n_1 = 300$, $n_2 = 200$: p-value ≈ 0.007 — significant.**
- The **larger samples (b) give the stronger evidence** — the same 0.10
  difference is much harder to explain by chance with ten times the data.

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.DataFrame({

    "Sample sizes": ["n1 = 30, n2 = 20", "n1 = 300, n2 = 200"],

    "Randomization p-value": [
        f"{rand_diff_p(24, 30, 14, 20):.3f}",
        f"{rand_diff_p(240, 300, 140, 200):.3f}",
    ],

}).to_string()
```

## Exercise 4.151

*(Skill Builder 2: many tests, all nulls true.)* 100 tests at a 5%
significance level: if every $H_0$ is true, each test still has a 5% chance
of rejecting by chance, so **about $100 \times 0.05 = 5$ of the tests will
incorrectly find significance**. The simulation below runs 10,000 tests in
which the null really is true (testing a mean with a randomization test)
and rejects 4.9% of them — right at the promised rate:

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
n, n_studies, chunk, reps = 20, 10000, 250, 1000
pvals = []
for start in range(0, n_studies, chunk):
    X = rng.standard_normal((chunk, n))            # data with H0 true
    obs = np.abs(X.mean(axis=1))
    signs = rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0], size=(chunk, reps, n))
    null = np.abs((X[:, None, :] * signs).mean(axis=2))
    pvals.append((null >= obs[:, None] - 1e-12).mean(axis=1))
pvals = np.concatenate(pvals)
f"Empirical Type I error rate over {n_studies} tests: {(pvals <= 0.05).mean():.3f} (nominal alpha = 0.05)"
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: p-values from 10000 tests in which the null hypothesis is true, with the 5 percent cutoff marked
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2.6))
sns.histplot(x=pvals, bins=20, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
ax.axvline(0.05, color="#c44e52", ls="--", lw=1.5)
ax.set_xlabel("p-value (null hypothesis true)")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of tests")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 4.152

*(Skill Builder 2)* 300 tests at a 1% significance level: each true null
has a 1% chance of a false rejection, so **about $300 \times 0.01 = 3$**
of the tests will incorrectly find significance. Even a strict level like
1% cannot protect a batch of hundreds of tests from yielding a few false
positives.

## Exercise 4.153

*(Skill Builder 2)* 40 tests at a 10% significance level: **about
$40 \times 0.10 = 4$** of the tests will incorrectly find significance.
A loose significance level produces false positives at a rate that adds up
quickly even in a modest batch of tests.

## Exercise 4.154

*(Skill Builder 2)* 800 tests at a 5% significance level: **about
$800 \times 0.05 = 40$** of the tests will incorrectly find significance.
The expected number of wrong conclusions grows with *both* the number of
tests and the significance level — a first warning about fishing for
significance in large batches.

## Exercise 4.155

**Interpreting a p-value.** Which statements are proper interpretations of
what a p-value measures?

- **(a) No.** The p-value is computed *assuming* $H_0$ is true; it says
  nothing about the probability that $H_0$ is true.
- **(b) No.** Same reason — the p-value is not the probability that $H_a$
  is true.
- **(c) Yes.** This is the definition: assuming $H_0$ is true, the
  probability of seeing a statistic as extreme as (or more extreme than)
  the one observed.
- **(d) No.** If $H_0$ is true, the probability of making a Type I error is
  the significance level $\alpha$ (the chance of rejecting a true null),
  not the p-value.
- **(e) No.** If $H_a$ is true, the probability of a Type II error is
  $\beta$, which depends on the true effect size and sample size — not the
  p-value.

## Exercise 4.156

**Translating information to other significance levels.** A two-tailed
test of $H_0: \rho = 0$ vs $H_a: \rho \neq 0$ rejects $H_0$ at the 5%
level (p-value $\le 0.05$). Which conclusions also definitely hold?

- **(a) Reject at a 1% level: not necessarily.** A p-value of, say, 0.03
  rejects at 5% but not at 1%; we only know p $\le 0.05$.
- **(b) Reject at a 10% level: definitely valid.** If p $\le 0.05$ then
  certainly p $\le 0.10$.
- **(c) Reject in favor of the one-tailed $H_a: \rho > 0$ at 5% (with
  positive sample correlation): definitely valid.** For the symmetric
  randomization distribution, the one-tailed p-value is half the two-tailed
  one, so it is at most $0.05/2 = 0.025 < 0.05$.

## Exercise 4.157

**Euchre.** Two teams play a series of games; the series stops when one
team is *statistically significantly* better than the other.

- **(a) Parameter:** $p$, the long-run proportion of games that team A
  would win against team B.
- **(b) Hypotheses:** $H_0: p = 0.5$ (the teams are equally good) vs
  $H_a: p \neq 0.5$ (one team is better — either one, so two-tailed).
- **(c) Statistic:** $\hat p$, the running proportion of games won by
  team A (recorded game by game as the series goes on).
- **(d) No.** After one or two games the evidence cannot possibly be
  strong: even two straight wins give a two-tailed p-value of
  $2(1/4) = 0.5$. Chance produces short winning streaks all the time, so
  the winner cannot be determined that quickly.
- **(e) The 1% level makes the series last longer.** Demanding stronger
  evidence (smaller $\alpha$) means waiting for a more extreme winning
  record — more games. (Note $\alpha$ here is exactly the chance of
  stopping the series and crowding a champion who is really no better.)

## Exercise 4.158

**Flying Home for the Holidays, On Time.** December flights: of 1000 Delta
flights, 45 arrived more than 30 minutes late; of 1000 United flights, 114
did. Is the proportion of over-30-minute-late flights different between the
airlines?

- **(a)** $H_0: p_U = p_D$ (the proportion of flights over 30 minutes late
  is the same for United and Delta) vs $H_a: p_U \neq p_D$ (the proportions
  differ — two-tailed).
- **(b)** The statistic recorded for each randomization sample is the
  difference in proportions $\hat p_U - \hat p_D$; for the observed sample
  it equals $114/1000 - 45/1000 = 0.114 - 0.045 = 0.069$.
- **(c)** The shuffle distribution (below, left) is centered at 0 with
  SE ≈ 0.012; the observed 0.069 lies far beyond every one of the 10,000
  shuffles — **p-value essentially 0**.
- **(d)** Since $0.0000 < \alpha = 0.01$: **reject $H_0$.** There is strong
  evidence that the proportion of flights arriving more than 30 minutes
  late differs between United and Delta (United's is higher).
- **(e) No — the conclusion changes.** With only 88 flights per airline but
  roughly the same proportions (10/88 vs 4/88), the observed difference is
  still about 0.068, but the shuffle distribution (below, right) is much
  wider and the p-value rises to about 0.17. At $\alpha = 0.01$ we **do not
  reject $H_0$**: smaller samples carry less information, and the same
  difference is no longer convincing.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Randomization distributions of the difference in late-flight proportions, full samples and samples of size 88
big = shuffle_diff_stats(114, 1000, 45, 1000)
small = shuffle_diff_stats(10, 88, 4, 88)
rand_plot([big, small], [114/1000 - 45/1000, 10/88 - 4/88],
          ["n = 1000 per airline", "n = 88 per airline"],
          "Randomization differences in proportions")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.DataFrame({
    "Sample sizes": ["1000 and 1000", "88 and 88"],
    "Observed statistic": [f"{114/1000 - 45/1000:.3f}", f"{10/88 - 4/88:.3f}"],
    "Two-tailed p-value": [f"{rand_diff_p(114, 1000, 45, 1000, two=True):.4f}",
                           f"{rand_diff_p(10, 88, 4, 88, two=True):.4f}"],
    "Reject at alpha = 0.01?": ["Yes", "No"],
}).to_string()
```

## Exercise 4.159

**Flaxseed and Omega-3.** A company advertises that its milled flaxseed
contains, on average, at least 3800 mg of ALA per tablespoon. Which
standard significance level — 1%, 5%, or 10% — makes most sense?

- **(a) 10%.** The company is running an internal double-check, is eager to
  find evidence *for* its own claim, and faces no real consequences either
  way; using a larger $\alpha$ makes it easier to find the evidence it
  hopes for, at little cost.
- **(b) 1%.** A consumer organization planning a lawsuit should demand very
  strong evidence before accusing the company: a small $\alpha$ keeps the
  risk of wrongly rejecting the claim (and triggering an unjustified suit)
  as low as possible.

## Exercise 4.160

**Dangerous new drug.** Testing whether a drug with potentially dangerous
side effects is significantly better than the current drug, where approval
means prescribing it to millions: use a **relatively small significance
level (such as $\alpha = 0.01$)**. A Type I error — switching millions of
patients to a drug that is not really better but has dangerous side
effects — is very costly, so strong evidence should be required first.

no consequences, while a small $\alpha$ would make it easy to miss anything

the Federal Trade Commission to file a lawsuit: use a **relatively small

supplement has significant health benefits: use a **relatively large

while a Type II error (failing to detect a real benefit) means missing out

## Exercise 4.165

**Expensive new drug.** A pharmaceutical company tests whether its new
(expensive) drug is significantly better than the existing drug:

- **The company would prefer a larger significance level** (such as 10%):
  it is easier to conclude that the new drug is better, which helps get it
  approved and sold at the higher price.
- **The consumer would prefer a smaller significance level** (such as 1%):
  switching to the pricier drug is only worthwhile if the improvement is
  real, so the consumer wants strong evidence that the new drug is actually
  better.

## Exercise 4.166

*(Type I and Type II errors in the situation of Exercise 4.160 — the new
drug with dangerous side effects.)* $H_0$: the new drug is not more
effective than the current one; $H_a$: it is.

- **Type I error:** concluding the new drug is better when it is not —
  millions of people are switched to a drug with dangerous side effects for
  no benefit. **Personally, this is the worse error** here.
- **Type II error:** failing to detect that the new drug really is better —
  patients keep using the old, less effective drug.

## Exercise 4.167

*(Errors in the situation of Exercise 4.161 — TV watching by sex.)*
$H_0$: there is no difference in the mean number of weekly TV hours between
male and female students; $H_a$: there is a difference.

- **Type I error:** concluding that male and female students differ in TV
  watching when, in the population, they do not.
- **Type II error:** failing to notice a difference that really exists.
- Which is worse is a matter of taste here — the stakes are trivial either
  way (a wrong claim in a class discussion vs a missed fun fact).

## Exercise 4.168

*(Errors in the situation of Exercise 4.162 — Wii bowling.)* $H_0$: my
average score is not higher than my friend's; $H_a$: mine is higher.

- **Type I error:** claiming I am the better bowler when, in the long run,
  I am not (bragging unjustifiably).
- **Type II error:** failing to detect that I really am better (forfeiting
  deserved bragging rights).

## Exercise 4.169

*(Errors in the situation of Exercise 4.163 — lying in advertising.)*
$H_0$: the company is not lying in its ads; $H_a$: the company is lying.

- **Type I error:** concluding the company is lying when it is not — a
  wrongful lawsuit against an honest company. **Personally, this is the
  worse error**: the accusation itself does real damage.
- **Type II error:** failing to convict a company that is lying —
  consumers keep being misled.

## Exercise 4.170

*(Errors in the situation of Exercise 4.164 — the vitamin supplement.)*
$H_0$: the supplement has no health benefits; $H_a$: it has benefits.

- **Type I error:** concluding the supplement helps when it does not —
  people take a useless pill (a fairly harmless mistake, given no side
  effects).
- **Type II error:** missing a supplement that genuinely helps — people
  forgo a real health benefit. **Personally, this is the worse error** in
  this setting, which is exactly why a larger $\alpha$ made sense.

## Exercise 4.171

**Influencing voters.** Testing whether a recorded phone call is more
effective than a mailed flyer at gaining candidate support, with
$\alpha = 0.05$.

- **(a)** A p-value of 0.027 is below 0.05: **reject $H_0$** — the data
  provide evidence that the recorded phone call is more effective than the
  mailed flyer at winning voter support.
- **(b) A Type I error.** We rejected $H_0$, so if $H_0$ is actually true
  we have erred. Here that means concluding that the phone call is more
  effective when, in reality, it is not.
- **(c)** A p-value of 0.18 is above 0.05: **do not reject $H_0$** — there
  is no evidence that the recorded phone call is more effective than the
  flyer.
- **(d) A Type II error.** We failed to reject $H_0$, so if $H_a$ is
  actually true we have erred. Here that means missing a real advantage of
  the phone call and concluding there is no difference when there is one.

## Exercise 4.172

**Significant and insignificant results.**

- **(a) Significant results (we rejected $H_0$):** two possible realities —
  (i) $H_0$ is actually false and we are right (a correct conclusion), or
  (ii) $H_0$ is actually true and we have made a **Type I error**.
- **(b) Insignificant results (we did not reject $H_0$):** two possible
  realities — (i) $H_0$ is actually true and we are right, or (ii) $H_0$ is
  actually false and we have made a **Type II error**.
- **(c)** We can never know which reality holds because the truth about the
  population is never observed: the whole point of a test is that data are
  consistent with more than one reality. We can control the *long-run
  probabilities* of the errors ($\alpha$ and $\beta$), but for any single
  study the underlying truth stays hidden — that uncertainty is built into
  statistical inference.

## Exercise 4.173

**Weight loss program.** A company advertises an average first-month loss
of 8 pounds; the FTC will sue for false advertising if the average is
lower.

- **(a)** $H_0: \mu = 8$ (patrons lose an average of 8 pounds the first
  month) vs $H_a: \mu < 8$ (the average loss is less than advertised).
- **(b)** With $\bar x = 7.9$ and p-value 0.006: reject $H_0$ at any usual
  level — the result is **statistically significant**, and the FTC has
  strong evidence that the mean weight loss is less than the advertised
  8 pounds.
- **(c) Not practically significant.** The estimated mean is 7.9 pounds vs
  the advertised 8.0 — a tenth of a pound, which no patron would notice or
  care about. With a very large sample, even trivially small differences
  become statistically significant; the p-value measures the strength of
  *evidence against $H_0$*, not the *size or importance* of the effect.
  A lawsuit over 0.1 pounds would be a poor use of "significance."

## Exercise 4.174

**Do iPads help kindergartners learn: a subtest.** In the Auburn, Maine
experiment, half the kindergarten classes got iPads in September and the
rest in December; the test compares mean scores on the HRSIW subtest.

- **(a)** Let $\mu_I$ and $\mu_C$ be the mean HRSIW scores (for all
  kindergarten children in settings like these) with the iPads
  (intervention) and without them (control). $H_0: \mu_I = \mu_C$ vs
  $H_a: \mu_I > \mu_C$.
- **(b)** p-value = 0.02 < 0.05: **reject $H_0$** — the results are
  statistically significant at the 5% level, providing evidence that the
  iPad group scored higher on the HRSIW subtest than the control group.
- **(c)** The school board member means that an effect of about **two
  points** on this subtest is tiny in educational terms. Even though the
  difference is unlikely to be chance (statistically significant), it may
  be too small to matter for children's actual learning — or to justify
  the cost of iPads for every class. Statistical significance answers "is
  the effect real?", not "is the effect big enough to care about?"

## Exercise 4.175

**Do iPads help kindergartners learn: a series of tests.** The HRSIW result
was significant, but it was 1 of 10 subtests tested (the other 9 were not
significant).

- If iPads have **no** effect at all, each of the 10 tests at
  $\alpha = 0.05$ still has a 5% chance of a false positive, so about
  $10 \times 0.05 = 0.5$ significant results are expected by chance, and
  the chance of at least one is $1 - 0.95^{10} \approx 0.40$.
- Seeing exactly **one significant result out of ten** is precisely the
  pattern that chance produces when nothing is going on. Before buying
  iPads for all kindergartners, we should hesitate: the single hit may well
  be a Type I error among the many tests, and genuine effects would more
  convincingly show up across several subtests.

## Exercise 4.176

**Vitamin C for sepsis.** A randomized experiment compared high-dose
intravenous vitamin C to a placebo in sepsis patients; many outcomes were
measured.

- **(a)** The test that was **not** significant (days on a ventilator) goes
  with **p = 0.15**, and the test that **was** significant (days out of the
  ICU) goes with **p = 0.03** — only 0.03 falls below the 0.05 threshold
  (0.15 does not).
- **(b)** In all, 46 tests were run and only 3 were significant at 5%. If
  vitamin C has no effect, chance alone produces about
  $46 \times 0.05 = 2.3$ significant results — almost exactly the 3
  observed. So the significant hits are about what randomness predicts, and
  we should hesitate to credit vitamin C for them (the classic
  multiple-testing trap).

## Exercise 4.177

**Impact of arts education.** A randomized experiment with over 10,000
students produced 72 hypothesis tests (6 outcomes × 12 groups) about the
impact of arts education.

- **(a)** If arts education has no effect, at the 5% level we expect about
  $72 \times 0.05 = \mathbf{3.6}$ significant tests just by chance; at the
  1% level, about $72 \times 0.01 = \mathbf{0.72}$.
- **(b)(i) Absences, math, reading, science (48 tests):** 1 significant at
  5% vs 2.4 expected, 0 at 1% vs 0.48 expected — **fewer than chance**.
  No, increased arts education does not appear to have an impact in these
  areas.
- **(b)(ii) Discipline and writing (24 tests):** 15 significant at 5% vs
  1.2 expected, 6 at 1% vs 0.24 expected — **far more than chance**. Yes,
  the evidence here goes well beyond what randomness would produce, so
  arts education does appear to have a real (positive) impact on discipline
  and writing.

## Exercise 4.178

**Eating breakfast cereal and conceiving boys.** Researchers tested 133
foods for a difference in the proportion conceiving boys; only breakfast
cereal was significant, at $\alpha = 0.01$.

- **(a)** If none of the foods has any effect, each test at 1% still has a
  1% chance of a false positive, so about $133 \times 0.01 = \mathbf{1.33}$
  — roughly one (possibly two) of the 133 foods — would be expected to show
  significance just by chance. Note the hint's point: the *small*
  significance level, not the number of foods, drives this expectation.
- **(b) Possibly, and we cannot rule it out.** One significant food out of
  133 tests is exactly the pattern chance is expected to produce (about
  1.33 hits), so a Type I error on cereal is a very live possibility — we
  simply cannot know from this study alone.
- **(c) No.** Even granting that the association is real, the study is
  **observational** — women chose their own diets. Cereal eaters may differ
  from non-eaters in many other ways (overall diet, income, lifestyle), so
  the headline's causal wording ("boost chances") overreaches: an
  association between cereal and boy births does not show that cereal
  *causes* boys.

## Exercise 4.179

**Approval from the FDA for antidepressants.** The FDA requires two
significant results (at 5%) from randomized double-blind experiments but
puts no limit on how many times a company can try.

- If the drug is useless, every single trial still has a 5% chance of a
  false positive. Over many tries the false positives pile up: about
  $0.05 \times (\text{number of trials})$ of them will be "significant,"
  and the chance of eventually collecting two grows with every retry —
  after 20 trials, for instance, the probability of at least two
  significant results is about 0.26 (computed below).
- So under the current rule, a company that simply keeps running trials
  will, with high probability, eventually get its two hits — even for a
  drug that does nothing. The FDA might require **all** trials to be
  reported, cap the number of attempts, pre-register trials, or tighten the
  criterion to account for the number of tries.

```{python}
#| echo: false
f"P(at least 2 of 20 independent trials significant at 5% | drug useless) = {1 - 0.95**20 - 20 * 0.05 * 0.95**19:.2f}"
```

## Exercise 4.180

**Does massage really help reduce inflammation in muscles?** The headline
result (reduced interleukin-6 at 2.5 hours, significant at 5%) came from a
study that actually ran 42 tests: 21 compounds × 2 times.

- **(a) Yes, we should have less confidence.** With 42 tests at 5%, chance
  alone produces about $42 \times 0.05 = 2.1$ significant results — so the
  single highlighted result could easily be one of those chance hits rather
  than a real effect.
- **(b) No.** Sixteen tests on muscle metabolites produced **zero**
  significant results — exactly consistent with massage having no effect on
  metabolites. (No false accusations needed here: nothing was found.)
- **(c) Reasonably safe, yes.** Eight tests on inflammation produced
  **four** significant results — vastly more than the
  $8 \times 0.05 = 0.4$ expected by chance. Such a cluster is unlikely to
  be a randomness fluke, so massage plausibly does reduce muscle
  inflammation (ideally we would also check that the significant tests
  point consistently in the anti-inflammatory direction).

## Exercise 4.181

**Cat ownership and schizophrenia.** Exercise 4.146 found an association
between childhood cat ownership and later schizophrenia; the same paper
provided three datasets (Table 4.15). Testing $H_0: p_S = p_C$ vs
$H_a: p_S > p_C$ (higher proportion of cat owners among schizophrenics)
for each dataset:

| Year | Schizophrenics | Controls |
|---|---|---|
| 1982 | 1075/2125 = 0.506 | 2065/4847 = 0.426 |
| 1992 | 84/165 = 0.509 | 65/165 = 0.394 |
| 1997 | 136/262 = 0.519 | 220/522 = 0.421 |

- **(a) Yes, it strengthens credibility.** Statistics naturally vary from
  sample to sample, but all three datasets point the same way (about 0.51
  vs about 0.42). Consistency across independent samples, collected in
  different years with different control groups, makes a fluke in any one
  dataset less plausible — this is replication working as intended.
- **(b)** The randomization p-values (below) are **1982: essentially 0;
  1992: ≈ 0.023; 1997: ≈ 0.006.**
- **(c) Yes, all three are significant at the 5% level** — and that
  **decreases** the suspicion that any single result was a Type I error:
  chance would rarely misfire the same way three independent times.
- **(d) Sample size, not the difference, drives these p-values.** The 1982
  dataset is huge ($n = 2125 + 4847$), so its standard error is tiny and
  even the smallest difference (0.080) sits far in the tail — the lowest
  p-value. The 1992 dataset is small ($n = 165 + 165$), so its standard
  error is large and even the biggest difference (0.115) is only
  moderately extreme — the highest p-value.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Randomization distributions of the difference in proportions of cat owners, schizophrenics minus controls, for the three datasets

s92 = shuffle_diff_stats(84, 165, 65, 165)
s97 = shuffle_diff_stats(136, 262, 220, 522)

          [1075/2125 - 2065/4847, 84/165 - 65/165, 136/262 - 220/522],
          ["1982: p = 0.000", "1992: p = 0.023", "1997: p = 0.006"],
          "Randomization differences in proportions", figsize=(7, 2.8))
```

## Exercise 4.182

**Mating choice and offspring fitness.** The original *Nature* study
concluded that mate choice increases offspring fitness in fruit flies
(p < 0.02); a replication experiment gave 10,000 larvae per group: 6067
survived with mate choice, 5976 without.

- **(a)** Testing $H_0: p_C = p_{NC}$ vs $H_a: p_C > p_{NC}$ with
  $\hat p_C - \hat p_{NC} = 0.6067 - 0.5976 = 0.0091$: the shuffle
  distribution has SE ≈ 0.0069, and the p-value is **≈ 0.10** (below).
- **(b)** Since $0.10 > \alpha = 0.05$: **do not reject $H_0$.** This
  replication provides no evidence that mate choice improves offspring
  fitness.
- **(c)** Treating each of the 50 runs as a case, the response is the
  per-run difference (Choice − NoChoice) in surviving larvae
  (`MateChoice` data, loaded below): $\bar x_d = 1.82$ larvae with
  $s = 15.8$. Randomizing the signs of the 50 differences gives a p-value
  of **≈ 0.21** for $H_0: \mu_d = 0$ vs $H_a: \mu_d > 0$.
- **(d)** Since $0.21 > 0.05$: **do not reject $H_0$** — no evidence that
  the average per-run difference is greater than 0.
- **(e) Type II error.** If mate choice really does improve fitness
  ($H_a$ true) and the follow-up study failed to reject $H_0$, it missed a
  real effect.
- **(f) Type I error.** If mate choice really does not help ($H_0$ true)
  and the original *Nature* study rejected $H_0$, it found significance
  that was not real — exactly why the controversial result needed the
  replication in the first place.

*Data:* `data/ch04/MateChoice.csv`, from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/MateChoice.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Shuffle distribution for the pooled larva counts and the distribution of the 50 per-run survival differences
mc = pd.read_csv("data/ch04/MateChoice.csv")
diffs = mc["Difference"].to_numpy(float)
pooled = shuffle_diff_stats(6067, 10000, 5976, 10000)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7, 2.8))
sns.histplot(x=pooled, bins=30, ax=axes[0], color="#4c72b0")
axes[0].axvline(6067/10000 - 5976/10000, color="#c44e52", lw=2)
axes[0].set_title("Shuffle p-hat difference (p = 0.10)", fontsize=10)
axes[0].set_xlabel("Randomization differences in proportions")
sns.histplot(x=diffs, bins=15, ax=axes[1], color="#4c72b0")
axes[1].axvline(diffs.mean(), color="#c44e52", lw=2)
axes[1].set_title("50 per-run differences (p = 0.21)", fontsize=10)
axes[1].set_xlabel("Choice minus NoChoice larvae")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
```

## Exercise 4.183

**Mating choice and offspring fitness: mini-experiments.** The replication
was actually a series of experiments, each made of 50 mini-experiments
(runs), 10 per day for 5 days.

- **(a)** If mate choice has no impact, each of the 50 runs at
  $\alpha = 0.05$ still has a 5% chance of significance, so **about
  $50 \times 0.05 = 2.5$** of the 50 p-values would be significant by
  chance.
- **(b)** Scanning the 50 p-values below: **8 are significant at 0.05**
  (0.01 on day 2; 0.02, 0.00, 0.01, 0.00 on day 3; 0.01 on day 4; 0.03 and
  0.02 on day 5) — more than the 2.5 expected, but scattered, not a
  consistent story.
- **(c) No — neither appropriate nor ethical.** Reporting only the single
  run with p = 0.0001, after having seen all 50 results, is cherry-picking
  (p-hacking): it hides the 49 runs that found nothing and presents a
  chance-selected extreme as if it were the whole story. The honest
  analysis combines all 50 runs — which, as Exercise 4.182 showed, show no
  effect — and selective reporting of this kind misleads readers about the
  actual weight of evidence.
- **(d) Yes.** A p-value near 1.00 for $H_a: p_C > p_{NC}$ means the run's
  data fell at the extreme *opposite* end of the randomization
  distribution. For the opposite alternative $H_a: p_C < p_{NC}$ those same
  two runs give p-values near 0 — apparently highly significant evidence
  that *preventing* mate choice improves fitness. The two "1.00" runs are
  the mirror image of the tiny p-values: extreme results, whichever way
  they point.
- **(e)** With 50 tests and no real effect, about 2.5 significant results
  are expected by chance, and if there is a tiny effect only some runs are
  lucky enough to detect it. A handful of tiny p-values scattered among
  mostly large ones — sometimes pointing each way — is exactly what many
  small noisy tests look like, so contradictory conclusions across runs
  are unsurprising: the multiple-testing problem guarantees mixed results.
- **(f)** Replication is the immune system of science: repeating a study in
  a different setting, with different researchers (and here, different
  mutant competitors and species), guards against Type I errors, sampling
  flukes, and over-generalization from one context. When replications
  agree — as in Exercise 4.181 — trust grows; when they contradict each
  other — as here — that too is informative, revealing that an effect is
  fragile or context-dependent and that no single study (even a *Nature*
  paper) should be taken at face value.

